To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
retinal ischemia and reperfusion result in lower levels of the three PKC isoforms, PKCα, -β1, and -β2, in both the neuro-retina and retinal artery.
retinal ischemia followed reperfusion results to a slight decrease of protein kinase C in both the retinas and retinal arteries.

retinal ischemia followed 5, 10, or 20 hours later by reperfusion resulted in a decrease in PKC in both porcine retinas and retinal arteries, and that the PKCs were expressed in the endothelium and the smooth muscle of the retinal artery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the intracellular pathways activated in retinopathy.
the development of novel pharmacological agents for the treatment of retinal vascular disorders.
the development of new therapeutic strategies in the treatment of ischemic retinopathy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
retinal ischemia and reperfusion results not only in a decreased protein expression of PKC in the retina, but also in the retinal arteries.
PKCα, -β1, and -β2 are expressed in both the retinas and arteries of the porcine eye.
retinal ischemia/reperfusion results in a down-regulation of the PKC system, which is more pronounced in the retinal arteries than in the neuroretina.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retinal vasulature can be studied separately from the retinal neuroretina.
PKC is involved in the ischemia-reperfused retina and that the retinal vasulature is a good model to study this.
PKC is involved in retinal ischemic injury, but that the role may be complex, with PKC being both protective and damaging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the retinal arteries are an important target for pharmacological treatment in the context of retinal circulatory disorders.

retinal ischemia followed reperfusion results not only in a reduction of PKCα and PKCβ1 mRNA and protein levels in the neuroretina, but also in the retinal arteries, suggesting that PKC may be a target for pharmacological treatment of circulatory failure.
